claim: The number of afferent synapses per IHC is unchanged in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: The number of afferent synapses per IHC was determined by the count of postsynaptic densities (PSDs) identified as PSD-95 immunofluorescent spots (Figure 1C,D,E) and was unchanged when RIBEYE was removed (13.7 ± 0.8, S.D. = 2.04; n = 56 cells, N = 4 in RBEKO/KO vs. 12.9 ± 0.6, S.D. = 2.13; n = 55 cells, N = 5 in RBEWT/WT).
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence data showing comparable numbers of PSD-95 immunofluorescent spots between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs

claim: Bassoon remains present at ribbonless afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Bassoon (Figure 1C) and RIM2 (Figure 1D), both presynaptic scaffold proteins (Khimich et al., 2005;Jung et al., 2015a), remained present at the ribbonless afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs (marked by PSD-95).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging showing bassoon co-localization with PSD-95 at RBEKO/KO IHC synapses, with citation to previous characterization of bassoon as presynaptic scaffold protein

claim: RIM2 remains present at ribbonless afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Bassoon (Figure 1C) and RIM2 (Figure 1D), both presynaptic scaffold proteins (Khimich et al., 2005;Jung et al., 2015a), remained present at the ribbonless afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs (marked by PSD-95).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging showing RIM2 co-localization with PSD-95 at RBEKO/KO IHC synapses, with citation to previous characterization of RIM2 as presynaptic scaffold protein

claim: Piccolino is absent from afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: The scaffold protein piccolino, the short isoform of piccolo (Regus-Leidig et al., 2013) that is present in cochlear and retinal ribbons (Khimich et al., 2005; tom Dieck et al., 2005; Regus-Leidig et al., 2013), was absent from afferent synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing absence of piccolino at afferent synapses, with citations to previous studies identifying piccolino in ribbons

claim: PSD areas are significantly increased in RBEKO/KO IHCs compared to RBEWT/WT IHCs.
source: The PSD areas were calculated by fitting a 2-dimensional Gaussian function to each PSD-95 immunofluorescent spot, revealing a significant increase in the RBEKO/KO condition (2.82 ± 0.09 µm², S.D. = 1.25; n = 178 spots, N = 3 vs. 1.74 ± 0.05 µm², S.D. = 0.58; n = 163 spots, N = 3 in RBEWT/WT IHCs; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon; Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of PSD-95 immunofluorescence showing statistically significant increase in PSD area in RBEKO/KO

claim: RBEKO/KO IHC synapses completely lack synaptic ribbons as shown by electron microscopy.
source: Random ultrathin (70–75 nm) sections prepared from P21 mice (two animals per genotype) after aldehyde fixation and conventional embedding procedures showed that IHCs from RBEKO/KO mice completely lack synaptic ribbons, while RBEWT/WT and heterozygous RBEWT/KO typically display one ribbon per AZ (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Transmission electron microscopy data from random sections showing absence of ribbons in RBEKO/KO IHCs

claim: Ribbons of RBEWT/KO IHCs are smaller in height, width and area compared to RBEWT/WT IHC synaptic ribbons.
source: Interestingly, ribbons of RBEWT/KO IHCs were smaller in height, width and area compared to RBEWT/WT IHC synaptic ribbons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C; ribbon height: 118.32 ± 3.17 nm, S.D. = 31.84 nm; n = 101 ribbons, N = 2 for RBEWT/KO vs. 197.09 ± 4.36 nm, S.D. = 44.93 nm; n = 106 ribbons, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; ribbon width: 119.80 ± 6.23 nm, S.D. = 62.27 nm for RBEWT/KO vs. 168.34 ± 6.83 nm, S.D. = 70.27 nm for RBEWT/WT; ribbon area: 11.5e3 ± 6.2e2 nm2, S.D. = 6.3e3 nm² for RBEWT/KO vs. 25.4e3 ±1.1e2 nm2, S.D. = 1.1e3 nm² for RBEWT/WT; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test for all)
evidence: Quantitative electron microscopy measurements showing statistically significant reductions in ribbon dimensions in heterozygous mice

claim: RBEKO/KO IHC synapses display multiple presynaptic densities (PDs) per active zone.
source: Random sections of synaptic contacts of RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 2C) often showed more than one presynaptic density (PD), each associated with a cluster of synaptic vesicles (henceforth considered individual AZs).
evidence: Electron microscopy observations showing multiple PDs at RBEKO/KO synapses

claim: RBEKO/KO IHC synapses at 6 weeks and 8 months of age show multiple AZs per contact, arguing against a developmental delay.
source: Moreover, we found more than one PD per synaptic contact in IHCs of older RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 2E,F; 6 weeks and 8 months, respectively), arguing against a delayed synaptic maturation to be the cause of the phenotype.
evidence: Electron microscopy data from older mice showing persistent multi-AZ phenotype, used to infer that this is not a developmental delay

claim: Serial 3D reconstructions of RBEKO/KO IHC synapses show on average 1.92 PDs per contact.
source: Analysis based on serial 3D reconstructions of synaptic contacts of RBEKO/KO IHCs from P21 animals showed on average 1.92 ± 0.34 PDs (S.D. = 1.16; n = 17 serial 3D reconstructions, N = 2) and 20.58 ± 2.98 total SVs per contact, S.D. = 10.34 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of serial 3D reconstructions from electron microscopy

claim: The lateral extent of individual PDs is comparable between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT synapses.
source: The lateral extent of the individual PDs, determined in random sections, was comparable between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT synapses (129.89 ± 2.53 nm, S.D. = 26.26 nm; n = 108 PDs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 129.35 ± 4.89 nm, S.D. = 50.86 nm; n = 108 PDs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; p=0.92, NPMC test)
evidence: Quantitative electron microscopy measurements with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: PSDs are significantly larger at RBEKO/KO synapses compared to RBEWT/KO PSDs.
source: PSDs tended to be increased in length at RBEKO/KO synapses compared to RBEWT/WT PSDs and were significantly larger than RBEWT/KO PSDs (Figure 2N; 623.77 ± 26.70 nm, S.D. = 264.33 nm; n = 98 PSDs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 555.91 ± 22.24 nm, S.D. = 236.42 nm; n = 113 PSDs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT vs. 521.34 ± 24.20 nm, S.D. = 242.03 nm; n = 100 PSDs, N = 2 for RBEWT/KO; p=0.01 for RBEKO/KO vs. RBEWT/KO, Tukey's test)
evidence: Quantitative electron microscopy measurements with statistical comparison

claim: Membrane-proximal SVs (MP-SVs) per AZ are significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO IHCs compared to RBEWT/WT.
source: We found both MP-SVs (Figure 2O; 1.92 ± 0.09, S.D. = 0.93; n = 108 AZs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 2.99 ± 0.12, S.D. = 1.18; n = 101 AZs, N = 2 for RBEWT/KO vs. 2.77 ± 0.12, S.D. = 1.18; n = 106 AZs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; p<0.0001 for RBEKO/KO vs. RBEWT/WT, NPMC test)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of random electron microscopy sections with statistical comparison

claim: PDA-SVs (PD-associated SVs) of individual ribbonless IHC AZs of RBEKO/KO mice are significantly fewer than RA-SVs (ribbon-associated SVs) at RBEWT/WT AZs.
source: and PDA-SVs (Figure 2P; 4.12 ± 0.15, S.D. = 1.50; n = 108 AZs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 10.09 ± 0.27, S.D. = 2.75; n = 106 AZs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; p<0.0001, Tukey's test) of the individual ribbonless IHC AZs of RBEKO/KO mice to be significantly fewer than the corresponding number of MP-SVs and RA-SVs counted at RBEWT/WT AZs.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of random electron microscopy sections with statistical comparison

claim: The fraction of PDA-SVs relative to total SVs at RBEKO/KO AZs is less than that of RA-SVs at RBEWT/WT AZs.
source: The fraction of PDA-SVs relative to the total number of SVs at RBEKO/KO AZs was less than that of RA-SVs at RBEWT/WT AZs (Figure 2Q; 0.67 ± 0.02, S.D. = 0.16; n = 108 AZs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 0.78 ± 0.01, S.D. = 0.08; n = 106 AZs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; p<0.0001, NPMC test).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of random electron microscopy sections with statistical comparison

claim: The fraction of MP-SVs at RBEKO/KO AZs is increased compared to RBEWT/WT AZs.
source: Consequently, we observed an increase in the fraction of MP-SVs at RBEKO/KO AZs (Figure 2Q; 0.33 ± 0.02, S.D. = 0.16; n = 108 AZs, N = 2 for RBEKO/KO vs. 0.22 ± 0.01, S.D. = 0.08; n = 106 AZs, N = 2 for RBEWT/WT; p<0.0001, NPMC test).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of random electron microscopy sections with statistical comparison

claim: Electron tomography confirmed the absence of synaptic ribbons and the presence of multiple AZs per contact in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Tomography confirmed the absence of synaptic ribbons and the presence of multiple AZs per contact, each with a clear PD (Figure 3B,D,F).
evidence: Electron tomography data corroborating findings from random sections

claim: The number of MP-SVs per AZ is significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO IHCs as shown by electron tomography.
source: We found a significant reduction in the number of MP-SVs per AZ in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 3J; RBEKO/KO = 6.30 ± 0.86, S.D. = 2.87 MP-SVs; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT = 8.70 ± 0.82, S.D. = 2.45 MP-SVs; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p=0.04, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; significant also by the second analysis method: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, supplementary file 1)
evidence: Quantitative electron tomography analysis with statistical comparison

claim: The fraction of tethered MP-SVs is not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: while the fraction of tethered MP-SVs (No. of tethered MP-SVs/No. of all MP-SVs) was not significantly altered (Figure 3K; RBEKO/KO = 0.75 ± 0.07, S.D. = 0.24; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT = 0.65 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.18; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p=0.30, t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative electron tomography analysis with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: The fraction of MP-SVs with multiple (≥2) tethers is significantly larger in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: The fraction of MP-SVs with multiple (≥2) tethers was significantly larger in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 3K; single-tethered MP-SVs: RBEKO/KO = 0.55 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.19; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT = 0.61 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.17; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p=0.81; multiple-tethered MP-SVs: RBEKO/KO = 0.20 ± 0.05, S.D. = 0.15; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT = 0.04 ± 0.02, S.D. = 0.05; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p=0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative electron tomography analysis with statistical comparison

claim: The number of PDA-SVs per RBEKO/KO AZ is smaller than that of RA-SVs at RBEWT/WT AZs as shown by electron tomography.
source: Further, and in line with analysis of random sections, the number of PDA-SVs per RBEKO/KO AZ was smaller than that of RA-SVs at RBEWT/WT AZs (Figure 3O; RBEKO/KO: 9.30 ± 1.13, S.D. = 3.74 PDA-SVs; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT: 30.33 ± 3.00, S.D. = 9.01 RA-SVs; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative electron tomography analysis with statistical comparison

claim: The fraction of PDA-SVs tethered to the PD is not different from that of RA-SVs tethered to the ribbon.
source: However, the fraction of PDA-SVs tethered to the PD was not different from that of RA-SVs tethered to the ribbon (Figure 3P; RBEKO/KO: 0.80 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.19 tethered PDA-SV fraction; n = 11 AZs, N = 3 vs. RBEWT/WT: 0.70 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.17 tethered RA-SV fraction; n = 9 AZs, N = 3; p=0.12, t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative electron tomography analysis with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: CaV1.3 Ca2+-channels remain clustered at RBEKO/KO AZs.
source: CaV1.3 Ca2+-channels remained clustered at RBEKO/KO AZs and were identified as CaV1.3 labeling juxtaposed to PSD-95 immunofluorescent spots (Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showing CaV1.3 clustering at synapses in RBEKO/KO

claim: Over 70% of RBEKO/KO synapses show smaller, rounder and often several Ca2+-channel clusters and PDs per synaptic contact.
source: While more than 80% of the RBEWT/WT synapses showed the typical stripe-like co-alignment of CaV1.3 and bassoon immunofluorescence (Neef et al., 2018), imaging of RBEKO/KO synapses indicated a high prevalence (over 70%) of smaller, rounder and often several Ca2+-channel clusters and PDs per synaptic contact (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: STED super-resolution immunofluorescence microscopy data with citation to previous characterization of normal synapse morphology

claim: Over 60% of RBEKO/KO synapses contain two or more Ca2+-channel clusters.
source: While more than 80% of RBEWT/WT synapses displayed a single cluster, over 60% of the RBEKO/KO synapses contained two or more Ca2+-channel clusters (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of STED immunofluorescence imaging

claim: The average number of CaV1.3-immunofluorescent structures is significantly higher at RBEKO/KO synapses compared to RBEWT/WT.
source: Hence, the average number of CaV1.3-immunofluorescent structures was significantly higher at RBEKO/KO synapses compared to RBEWT/WT (2.06 ± 0.09, S.D. = 1.16; n = 178 spots, N = 3 vs. 1.16 ± 0.03, S.D. = 0.38; n = 183 spots, N = 2; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of STED immunofluorescence imaging with statistical comparison

claim: The amplitude of Ca2+-influx is unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: The amplitude of Ca2+-influx (Figure 5Ai; for Ca2+-current density, see Figure 5Aii) was unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs (-151 ± 12.9 pA, S.D. = 59 pA; n = 21 IHCs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO vs. -161 ± 15.4 pA, S.D. = 71 pA; n = 21 IHCs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT; p=0.62, t-test)
evidence: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: Kinetics of Ca2+-channel activation are unchanged in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Kinetics of Ca2+-channel activation were unchanged (Figure 5B)
evidence: Analysis of Ca2+-current kinetics from patch-clamp recordings

claim: Inactivation kinetics of Ca2+-channels are slightly faster in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: whereas inactivation kinetics were slightly faster in the RBEKO/KO IHCs (smaller residual Ca2+-current at 200 ms of depolarization (normalized to the peak current): 0.82 ± 0.007, S.D. = 0.02; n = 10 IHCs, N = 5 for RBEKO/KO vs. 0.85 ± 0.01, S.D. = 0.04; n = 11 IHCs, N = 7, in the RBEWT/WT condition; p=0.017, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 5D).
evidence: Analysis of Ca2+-current inactivation from patch-clamp recordings with statistical comparison

claim: The potential of half-maximal Ca2+-channel activation (Vh) is shifted by 2 mV to more depolarized potentials in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: When analyzing the voltage-dependence of Ca2+-channel activation (Figure 5C), we found a small (2 mV) but significant depolarizing shift of the potential of half-maximal Ca2+-channel activation, Vh (Figure 5Ci, −22.96 ± 0.43 mV, S.D. = 2.39 mV; n = 21 IHCs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO vs. −25.04 ± 0.65 mV, S.D. = 2.98 mV; n = 21 IHCs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT; p=0.017, t-test).
evidence: Analysis of voltage-dependence of Ca2+-channel activation from patch-clamp recordings with statistical comparison

claim: The average voltage-sensitivity of Ca2+-channel activation (slope factor k) is not altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: The average voltage-sensitivity of activation (slope factor k) was not altered (5 mM [Ca2+]e: p=0.67, t-test, Figure 5Cii).
evidence: Statistical analysis of voltage-sensitivity parameter from patch-clamp recordings showing no significant difference

claim: Maximal amplitudes of synaptic Ca2+-influx (ΔF/F0) are comparable between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
source: We found comparable maximal amplitudes of the baseline-normalized fluorescence change (ΔF/F0, 0.88 ± 0.08, S.D. = 0.66; n = 61 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 7 for RBEKO/KO vs. 0.85 ± 0.08, S.D. = 0.68; n = 78 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 8 for RBEWT/WT; p=0.20, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 6C).
evidence: Confocal Ca2+-imaging data with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: The voltage for half-maximal activation (Vh) of synaptic Ca2+-influx is shifted by 5 mV to more depolarized potentials in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Analysis of fractional activation revealed a depolarized shift in Vh by on average 5 mV in RBEKO/KO IHCs (−22.76 ± 1.25 mV, S.D. = 9.26 mV; n = 55 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 7 for RBEKO/KO vs. −27.37 ± 0.90 mV, S.D. = 7.48 mV; n = 68 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 8 for RBE WT/WT; p=0.0029, t-test; Figure 6D,Di)
evidence: Analysis of voltage-dependence of synaptic Ca2+-signals from confocal imaging with statistical comparison

claim: The slope factor of voltage-dependent activation of synaptic Ca2+-influx is unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: while the slope factor of voltage-dependent activation was unaltered (p=0.42, t-test, Figure 6Dii).
evidence: Statistical analysis of voltage-sensitivity parameter from Ca2+-imaging showing no significant difference

claim: The spatial extent of synaptic Ca2+-signals is greater at RBEKO/KO AZs compared to RBEWT/WT AZs.
source: Finally, we studied the spatial extent of the synaptic Ca2+-signals and estimated Full Width Half Maximum (FWHM) by fitting 2D Gaussian functions to the hotspots of Ca2+-indicator fluorescence and found a greater spread of Ca2+-signals at RBEKO/KO AZs (Figure 6E,F; long axis (L.A.) = 1317 ± 49 nm, S.D. = 384 nm, short axis (S.A.) = 906 ± 36 nm, S.D. = 284 nm; n = 61 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 7 vs. L.A. = 1083 ± 33 nm, S.D. = 283 nm; (p=0.00016, t-test), S.A. = 793 ± 27 nm, S.D. = 233 nm, (p=0.0029, t-test); n = 74 AZs in 15 IHCs, N = 8 for RBEWT/WT).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of Ca2+-imaging data with statistical comparison

claim: Immunofluorescence intensities of parvalbumin-α, calretinin and calbindin-28k are not significantly different between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
source: We did not find any significant differences in their immunofluorescence intensity between IHCs of both genotypes (in arbitrary units, parvalbumin intensity: 2.24 ± 0.15, S.D. = 1.04 for RBEKO/KO vs. 1.88 ± 0.15, S.D = 1.01 for RBEWT/WT, p=0.08; calbindin intensity: 0.82 ± 0.06, S.D. = 0.43 for RBEKO/KO vs.0.95 ± 0.07, S.D. = 0.49 for RBEWT/WT, p=0.23; calretinin intensity: 0.91 ± 0.04, S.D. = 0.26 for RBEKO/KO vs. 0.82 ± 0.04, S.D. = 0.28 for RBEWT/WT, p=0.09; n = 49 cells and N = 4 for both conditions, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test for all; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Semi-quantitative immunofluorescence analysis with statistical comparisons showing no significant differences

claim: Exocytic ΔCm in response to step-depolarizations to maximal Ca2+-influx (-14 mV) is not different between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
source: Using IHCs from 2/3-week-old RBEWT/WT and RBEKO/KO mice, we found that ΔCm in response to step-depolarizations to the potential that elicits maximal Ca2+-influx (−14 mV) were not different between IHCs with or without ribbons.
evidence: Perforated-patch whole-cell recordings of exocytic membrane capacitance changes

claim: Fast exocytosis elicited by depolarizations of up to 20 ms is unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Both, fast exocytosis elicited by depolarizations of up to 20 ms, attributed to the fusion of the readily releasable pool of SVs (RRP, Moser and Beutner, 2000), and longer stimuli, thought to reflect sustained exocytosis, ongoing SV replenishment and fusion, were unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7A,B,C).
evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements with citation to previous characterization of RRP

claim: Sustained exocytosis during longer stimuli is unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Both, fast exocytosis elicited by depolarizations of up to 20 ms, attributed to the fusion of the readily releasable pool of SVs (RRP, Moser and Beutner, 2000), and longer stimuli, thought to reflect sustained exocytosis, ongoing SV replenishment and fusion, were unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7A,B,C).
evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements with citation to previous characterization

claim: ΔCm induced by 20 ms long maximal Ca2+-influx is 16.70 ± 1.67 fF for RBEKO/KO compared to 15.22 ± 0.98 fF for RBEWT/WT.
source: On average, ΔCm induced by 20 ms long maximal Ca2+-influx was 16.70 ± 1.67 fF (S.D. = 5.80 fF; n = 12 cells, N = 7) for RBEKO/KO compared to 15.22 ± 0.98 fF (S.D. = 3.26 fF; n = 11 cells, N = 8) for RBEWT/WT.
evidence: Quantitative membrane capacitance measurements

claim: Exocytic ΔCm elicited by 200 ms long maximal Ca2+-influx is 62.09 ± 5.40 fF for RBEKO/KO versus 63.28 ± 6.64 fF for RBEWT/WT.
source: Exocytic ΔCm elicited by 200 ms long maximal Ca2+-influx (same IHCs as for 20 ms), on average, amounted to 62.09 ± 5.40 fF (S.D. = 18.70 fF) for RBEKO/KO versus 63.28 ± 6.64 fF (S.D. = 22.04 fF) for RBEWT/WT.
evidence: Quantitative membrane capacitance measurements

claim: Trains of 20 step-depolarizations do not reveal impaired exocytosis in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Moreover, trains of 20 step-depolarizations to −17 mV of 20 ms pulse duration did not reveal impaired exocytosis in RBEKO/KO IHCs, even when the inter-stimulus interval time was as short as 160 ms (Figure 7D; n = 11 cells, N = 5 for RBEWT/WT and n = 13 cells, N = 8 for RBEKO/KO).
evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements during repetitive stimulation

claim: RRP recovery from partial depletion is not altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs when probed with maximal Ca2+-influx.
source: We further explored RRP recovery from partial depletion using a paired-pulse protocol (two strong 20 ms depolarizations to −14 mV separated by 50, 110, 260 and 510 ms inter-pulse intervals; Figure 7E,F). RRP recovery, estimated as the ΔCm ratio of the second and the first pulse, was not altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs at least when probing RRP exocytosis with maximal Ca2+-influx from a hyperpolarized resting potential (Figure 7F).
evidence: Paired-pulse membrane capacitance measurements

claim: Exocytosis for stronger depolarizations (e.g., to -39 mV) is not significantly different between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
source: In agreement with the results obtained at maximal Ca2+-influx, we did not find significant differences in ΔCm for stronger depolarizations (e.g. pulses to −39 mV elicited an average ΔCm of 20.67 ± 7.46 fF, S.D. = 23.58 fF, nmin = 10 IHCs, N = 9 for RBEKO/KO vs. 24.12 ± 4.04 fF, S.D. = 13.98 fF, nmin = 10 IHCs, N = 9 for RBEWT/WT; p=0.20; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements at different depolarization potentials with statistical comparison

claim: Exocytosis for weaker depolarizations in the range of physiological receptor potentials is subtly but significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: However, for weaker depolarizations in the range of physiological receptor potentials (Russell and Sellick, 1983), we observed a subtle but significant reduction in exocytosis for RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7H, p=0.0115, p=0.0295 and p=0.1321 for −45, –43 and −41 mV; without definitive outliers as determined by Graphpad Prism: p=0.0017, p=0.0042 and p=0.0489, respectively; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test for all).
evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements at different depolarization potentials with statistical comparison and citation to previous characterization of physiological receptor potentials

claim: The amplitude of ABR wave I is significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: First, we recorded auditory brainstem responses (ABR) and found a significant reduction in the amplitude of wave I that reflects the SGN compound action potential (1.14 ± 0.13 µV, S.D. = 0.38 µV, N = 10 for RBEKO/KO vs. 3.30 ± 0.51 µV, S.D. = 1.54 µV, N = 10 for RBEWT/WT, p=0.0007, NPMC test).
evidence: ABR recordings with statistical comparison

claim: Reduced ABR wave I amplitude indicates less synchronous SGN activation in the absence of synaptic ribbons.
source: This indicates less synchronous SGN activation in the absence of synaptic ribbons (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Interpretation of ABR wave I amplitude reduction based on understanding of what wave I represents

claim: Subsequent ABR waves (II, IV and V) are normal in amplitude in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: The subsequent ABR waves (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) were normal in amplitude (waves II, IV and V, while wave III was reduced)
evidence: ABR recordings showing normal amplitudes for specific waves

claim: ABR wave III is reduced in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: The subsequent ABR waves (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) were normal in amplitude (waves II, IV and V, while wave III was reduced)
evidence: ABR recordings showing reduced amplitude for wave III

claim: Normal amplitudes of subsequent ABR waves indicate a degree of central auditory compensation for the sound encoding deficit.
source: indicating a degree of central auditory compensation for the sound encoding deficit, for example via coincidence detection of converging SGN input in the cochlear nucleus (Joris et al., 1994; Strenzke et al., 2009).
evidence: Interpretation of normal subsequent ABR waves with citations to previous work on central auditory processing

claim: Cochlear amplification is intact in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: Cochlear amplification, probed by recordings of distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAE, Figure 8D), was intact in RBEKO/KO mice.
evidence: DPOAE recordings showing normal cochlear amplification

claim: RBEWT/KO mice show no significant changes in ABR wave I amplitudes and ABR thresholds.
source: Additionally, RBEWT/KO mice showed no significant changes in ABR wave I amplitudes and ABR thresholds (Figure 8)
evidence: ABR recordings from heterozygous mice showing no significant differences

claim: There is an increased abundance of SGNs with low spontaneous firing rates in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: We first assessed the spontaneous firing activity and found an increased abundance of SGNs with low spontaneous firing rates in RBEKO/KO mice (72% with rates < 10 Hz, n = 43 SGNs, N = 9 vs. 50% in RBEWT/WT, n = 40 SGNs, N = 8; p=0.0267, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; Figure 9A).
evidence: Extracellular recordings from single SGNs with statistical comparison

claim: Frequency tuning is intact in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: Frequency tuning was intact in RBEKO/KO SGNs (Figure 9B): the sharpness of tuning expressed by the Q10dB (width of tuning curve 10 dB above threshold at the characteristic frequency (Cf) normalized by Cf) was comparable (mean: 9.28 ± 1.01, S.D. = 6.32 and median: 7.41 for RBEKO/KO SGNs, n = 39 SGNs, N = 9 vs. mean: 12.50 ± 1.98, S.D. = 11.91 and median: 8.36 for RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 36 SGNs, N = 9; p=0.28, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Analysis of frequency tuning curves from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claim: The sound threshold at characteristic frequency is significantly elevated by almost 20 dB in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: However, the sound threshold at Cf was significantly elevated by almost 20 dB in RBEKO/KO mice (35.60 ± 3.45 dB SPL, S.D. = 22.66 dB SPL for RBEKO/KO SGNs, n = 43 SGNs, N = 9 vs. 16.05 ± 2.47 dB SPL, S.D. = 15.42 dB SPL for RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 39 SGNs, N = 9, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 9C).
evidence: Analysis of sound thresholds from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claim: The threshold increase in RBEKO/KO SGNs seems unlikely to result from a functional cochlear deficit upstream of the IHCs given normal frequency tuning and DPOAE.
source: Given the normal frequency tuning and DPOAE, this threshold increase seems unlikely to result from a putative functional cochlear deficit upstream of the IHCs.
evidence: Inference based on combination of normal frequency tuning and DPOAE with elevated thresholds

claim: Peak firing rate at sound onset is reduced in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: We observed reduced spike rates of SGNs from RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 9D,E) both at sound onset (p=0.0001, n = 39 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 38 SGNs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT, t-test)
evidence: Analysis of PSTH from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claim: Adapted firing rate is reduced in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: We observed reduced spike rates of SGNs from RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 9D,E) both at sound onset (p=0.0001, n = 39 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 38 SGNs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT, t-test) and after short-term adaptation (p=0.0023, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Analysis of PSTH from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claim: The mean apparent adaptation time constant is significantly slowed in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: The mean apparent adaptation time constant reported by single-exponential fitting were significantly slowed in RBEKO/KO SGNs (9.83 ± 0.50 ms, S.D. = 2.85 ms, median: 10.46 ms, n = 32 SGNs, N = 8) as compared to RBEWT/WT SGNs (8.71 ± 0.50 ms, S.D. = 3.05 ms, median: 8.73 ms, n = 37 SGNs, N = 9, p=0.033, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Exponential fitting to PSTH data with statistical comparison

claim: First spike latency is prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: As expected for the reduced peak firing rate, we found prolonged first spike latency which also showed greater temporal jitter (Figure 9F).
evidence: Analysis of first spike timing from single SGN recordings

claim: First spike latency shows greater temporal jitter in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: As expected for the reduced peak firing rate, we found prolonged first spike latency which also showed greater temporal jitter (Figure 9F).
evidence: Analysis of first spike timing variability from single SGN recordings

claim: The reduced peak firing rate together with increased first spike latency jitter likely explain the reduction in ABR wave I amplitude.
source: The reduced peak firing rate together with increased first spike latency jitter likely explain the reduction in ABR wave I amplitude.
evidence: Inference connecting single SGN firing properties to ABR wave I amplitude

claim: The firing of putative AVCN neurons is better preserved than SGN firing in RBEKO/KO mice.
source: The firing of putative AVCN neurons was better preserved: putative bushy cells showed normal sound driven rates and chopper cells only a mild reduction in peak rate (Figure 10).
evidence: Extracellular recordings from cochlear nucleus neurons

claim: The spike rate increase with sound pressure level is not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: These 'rate-level functions' (Figure 11A) indicated that the spike rate increase with the sound pressure level (p=0.068, n = 24 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 19 SGNs, N = 7 in RBEWT/WT, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test, Figure 11—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Analysis of rate-level functions from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: The dynamic range of sound coding is not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: and the dynamic range of sound coding (sound pressure level for which the spike rate changes from 10–90%, Figure 11—figure supplement 1B, p=0.3044, t-test) were not significantly altered.
evidence: Analysis of dynamic range from rate-level functions with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claim: The maximal firing rate of RBEKO/KO SGNs is reduced when probed with transposed tones.
source: We then used transposed tones (Cf at 500 Hz modulation frequency) in order to probe for the temporal fidelity and reliability of firing in RBEKO/KO SGNs in the steady state (Figure 11D). These experiments corroborated the reduced maximal firing rate of RBEKO/KO SGNs (n = 22 SGNs, N = 7 in RBEKO/KO and n = 15 SGNs, N = 6 in RBEWT/WT, p<0.0001, t-test)
evidence: Analysis of responses to transposed tones with statistical comparison

claim: The temporal precision of sound coding is impaired in the steady state in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: and indicated that the temporal precision of sound coding is impaired also in the steady state (reduced Synchronization Index: p=0.0043, t-test).
evidence: Analysis of synchronization to transposed tones with statistical comparison

claim: The time constant of recovery from forward masking is prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
source: The time constant of recovery was prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs (90.80 ± 8.66 ms, S.D. = 45.00 ms, n = 27 SGNs, N = 8 vs. 33.53 ± 5.74 ms, S.D. = 28.11 ms, in RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 24 SGNs, N = 7, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test)
evidence: Exponential fitting to forward masking recovery data with statistical comparison

claim: Prolonged recovery from forward masking indicates slowed RRP replenishment in the absence of the ribbon.
source: indicating slowed RRP replenishment in the absence of the ribbon.
evidence: Interpretation of prolonged recovery time constant based on understanding of forward masking paradigm

claim: Biophysical modeling suggests that the total number of release sites (RRP) is only slightly reduced at ribbonless synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
source: Taken together the fits from forward masking and tone bursts suggest that the total number of release sites (RRP) was only slightly reduced at ribbonless synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
evidence: Results from biophysical modeling of SGN responses

claim: A strong firing response at sound onset requires longer recovery in RBEKO/KO, indicating more efficient SV replenishment in the presence of ribbons.
source: However, a strong firing response at sound onset, that is release of a large standing RRP, required longer recovery indicating more efficient SV replenishment in the presence of ribbons, which is reflected in the larger refilling rate constants estimated by the model of RBEWT/WT synapses.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results and experimental observations regarding recovery times

claim: RIBEYE is required for ribbon formation in mammalian IHCs.
source: Our work confirms the central role of RIBEYE for forming synaptic ribbons (Schmitz et al., 2000; Magupalli et al., 2008; Maxeiner et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary statement with citations to previous work establishing RIBEYE's role in ribbon formation

claim: The synaptic ribbon is important for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision at IHC synapses.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that the synaptic ribbon is important for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision at IHC synapses.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study

claim: The ribbon has a role in organizing the topography of the IHC active zone.
source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
evidence: Summary statement based on morphological findings showing multi-AZ organization in RBEKO/KO

claim: The ribbon has a role in Ca2+-channel regulation.
source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
evidence: Summary statement based on findings of altered Ca2+-channel voltage-dependence and spatial organization

claim: The ribbon has a role in vesicle replenishment.
source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
evidence: Summary statement based on findings of slowed recovery from adaptation and reduced vesicle pools

claim: The multi-AZ morphology of RBEKO/KO IHC synapses reflects a compensatory effort rather than developmental delay.
source: While we cannot rule out some sort of developmental delay of RIBEYE-deficient IHCs, we suspect that the morphological transformation into a multi-AZ morphology reflects a compensatory effort.
evidence: Interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence including persistence in older animals and mature synaptic features

claim: The loss of synaptic Ca2+-channels from bassoon-deficient ribbonless IHC synapses indicates a role of bassoon in promoting Ca2+-channel tethering at the AZ.
source: Therefore, the loss of synaptic Ca2+-channels from the bassoon-deficient ribbonless IHC synapses, indicates a role of bassoon in promoting Ca2+-channel tethering at the AZ likely via interaction with RIM-binding protein (Davydova et al., 2014), which was previously shown to interact with CaV1.3 Ca2+-channels (Hibino et al., 2002) and is required for establishing a normal Ca2+-channel complement of the IHC AZ (Krinner et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with bassoon mutants and citations to previous work on protein interactions

claim: The depolarized Vh-shift of synaptic Ca2+-influx is relevant for hair cell transmission.
source: A small, but significant reduction of exocytosis for weak depolarizations in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7, seen also in the accompanying paper by Becker et al.) suggests that the Vh shift is relevant for hair cell transmission (see also below).
evidence: Inference connecting the observed Vh shift to functional consequences in exocytosis

claim: Some features of the IHC ribbon-type AZ can be replaced by a ribbonless multi-AZ morphology.
source: In fact, our study of IHCs, unlike the situation for bipolar cell retinal ribbons (Maxeiner et al., 2016), suggests that some features of the IHC ribbon-type AZ can be very well replaced by a ribbonless multi-AZ morphology: the synaptic complement of Ca2+-channels and SVs, as well as exocytic ΔCm elicited by strong depolarizations, were similar.
evidence: Summary interpretation based on findings of normal Ca2+-channel numbers and exocytosis for strong stimuli, with citation to contrasting findings in retina

claim: The study likely underestimated the role of the ribbon due to substantial compensation.
source: Therefore, we likely underestimated the role of the ribbon in sound encoding in our present study.
evidence: Speculation based on observation of compensatory multi-AZ morphology

claim: Two mechanisms with likely additive effects explain impaired sound encoding despite unaltered exocytic ΔCm: the depolarized shift of synaptic Ca2+-channels and reduced SV-replenishment.
source: We propose two mechanisms with likely additive effects to explain this surprising finding: i) the small depolarized shift of synaptic Ca2+-channels might contribute the lower spontaneous and evoked firing rates as well as higher sound thresholds of SGNs and ii) the reduced SV-replenishment might not suffice to balance the rate of consumption leading to a smaller standing RRP in vivo, while the arrest of exocytosis in the voltage-clamped IHCs for tens of seconds likely enables complete filling of the release sites (max. standing RRP).
evidence: Proposed mechanistic explanation integrating multiple experimental findings
